levelMapping: Arista runs a deliberately flat ladder: almost everyone in India is hired with the title 'Software Engineer' regardless of YOE (a 2024 offer-holder: 'there is no concept of Senior Software Engineer'); recruiters and candidates informally call the 3-6 YOE band SDE-2, and a few 'Senior Software Engineer' reqs exist in Pune/Bengaluru. At ~3.3 YOE you interview for Software Engineer ≈ Google L4 scope. 2024-25 Bengaluru/Pune data points at ~3 YOE: ₹26-30L base + $20-25K RSU over 4 years + 3-4.5L anniversary bonus ≈ 37-46 LPA first year; at 4-4.5 YOE strong negotiators got 30-37L base + $68-70K RSU (~50-60 LPA). First offers are frequently lowballs (23L base at 3 YOE reported); counters moved base 23→27L+ — negotiate with competing offers.

process.summary: Arista's loop is fundamentals-heavy and C/C++-centric rather than pure LeetCode: every round mixes DSA (linked lists, BSTs, binary search, bit manipulation) with C/C++ pointer puzzles, output prediction, live debugging, OS internals and — for networking teams — protocol depth. Experienced hires usually see 2-4 rounds: a 60-90 min DSA+C round (full runnable code in CoderPad or an IDE, often against a pre-written test harness), a 60-120 min systems/OS/LLD round (sometimes debugging a program over SSH in vim), and a hiring-manager/director round that is a deep architecture discussion of your own project plus a design question; HR/offer discussion closes it. Verdicts are fast and binary, interviewers often skip introductions and demand working code (never pseudocode), and multiple candidates report rejection despite positive round feedback (director-level resume review is a real filter).

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.what: Outreach is usually inbound via LinkedIn or Naukri (often a third-party agency). Covers background, CTC expectation, notice period, team (EOS, SONiC, CloudVision/CV-CUE, UI) and loop logistics.
rounds.probes: One 2025 US candidate was explicitly warned the interviewers are 'picky'. Expectation setting: some loops end after one round; offers occasionally come on the spot after round 2.

rounds.name: Online assessment (HackerRank)
rounds.what: Universal for campus/intern and common off-campus even at 3-4 YOE (a 3-YOE 2026 candidate had a 4-section OA: 5 MCQs/5 min, 5 MCQs/15 min, 1 coding/25 min, 1 coding/30 min). MCQs cover C/C++ output tracing, pointers, OS (fork counts, FIFO page replacement, process states), hashing collisions, XOR/bit manipulation, time complexity and light aptitude; 2-3 coding problems at LC medium to medium-hard (priority queue, greedy, DP/knapsack, trees, LFU cache).
rounds.probes: Languages restricted to C/C++/Java — Python is disallowed. Recruiter-sourced experienced candidates frequently skip the OA and go straight to the technical screen.

rounds.name: Technical round 1 — DSA + C/C++
rounds.what: Two coding problems (linked lists, BSTs, binary search / rotated arrays, sliding window, bit manipulation) in CoderPad, Google Meet + IDE, or VS Code, frequently with a half-complete harness and test cases you must make pass. Interspersed C/C++ warm-ups: pointer-reseating puzzles, malloc/free questions, output prediction, runtime complexity.
rounds.probes: Complete runnable code is mandatory — interviewers run their own test cases and expect edge-case handling (double pointers, void return signatures, parent pointers). Some interviewers skip intros entirely and give no hints; complexity must be stated unprompted.

rounds.name: Technical round 2 — systems / OS / debugging / LLD
rounds.what: Varies by team: (a) OS deep dive — memory layout, stack overflow, virtual memory, implement free()/memcpy(), sometimes SSHing into a live Linux box to debug code in vim; (b) concurrency — find and fix a deadlock in a money-transfer snippet, producer-consumer; (c) LLD — license manager, parking lot, firewall; (d) networking depth for EOS/SONiC — VRF, TCAM/ACLs, packet walk-through, Linux network namespaces, plus a live C debugging exercise.
rounds.probes: Relentless 'why' follow-ups; constraints get changed mid-problem; a 2026 round-2 candidate: questions test 'basic reasoning ability and critical thinking rather than just solution'. Composure under live debugging is itself evaluated.

rounds.name: Hiring manager / Director round
rounds.what: Deep architecture discussion of your current project (tech choices, DB, failure handling), one design question (e-commerce, Coursera-like licensing platform, top-K log analysis), OS/C++ depth questions, and behavioral. The final director round is frequently in person in Bengaluru/Pune with travel reimbursed; strong candidates sometimes get the offer after round 2 with this round waived.
rounds.probes: Directors are technically deep — expect unordered_map internals, Linux questions, 'how would you find duplicate files in a directory', CAP/transactions if you claim backend experience. Director-level resume review can still reject you after positive interview feedback.

rounds.name: HR / offer discussion
rounds.what: Compensation, future plans, higher-studies question (campus). Negotiation round — initial numbers are often low.
rounds.probes: Multiple reports of hardball comp tactics: asking for raise letters/payslip proof after number agreement, refusing to move base, weeks of silence. Keep competing offers alive.

process.indiaNotes: India hires in Bengaluru and Pune (EOS, routing/PI, SONiC, CloudVision, UI teams); the pipeline is recruiter/Naukri outreach plus big on-campus drives. Title is flat 'Software Engineer' at nearly every YOE. The India loop is the same fundamentals-heavy format as US/EU but typically 3 rounds + HR, with the director round often in person (travel reimbursed for outstation candidates). US loops show the same C-coding screen plus a final with two back-to-back interviewers deliberating on the spot; Ireland/EU graduate loops are OA + technical + manager. India-specific friction reported 2024-26: ghosting after positive feedback, rejection via director resume review without round 2, a hiring freeze-period rule (one 2024 candidate was told a 2023 rejection permanently barred rehire; a 2026 frontend candidate was given a 1-year cool-off), and position-filled races favouring local candidates who can attend in-person rounds quickly.
process.timeline: Fast by default: Glassdoor averages ~10-14 days for Software Engineer, and campus loops finish OA→offer inside 2 days. Off-campus reports range from 2 to 6 weeks, with multi-week gaps between rounds (one candidate waited 3 weeks for an in-person round; another got round-2 confirmation 2 weeks after round 1).
tips: Write complete, runnable code and run it against the interviewer's tests — pseudocode is an instant negative; several rounds provide a harness whose tests must pass.
Drill C pointers until reflexive: pointer reseating (p=&x vs *p=x), returning stack addresses, sizeof(ptr) vs sizeof(array), double pointers (Node**), struct padding, malloc/calloc/free semantics.

Implement from scratch before the loop: linked-list ops (reverse in range, remove by value via Node**), BST ops with parent pointers (successor/predecessor/min/max/delete), a hash map, a dynamic array in C, free()/memcpy().

Revise OS cold: process memory layout, stack overflow, virtual memory, fork/exec, zombie vs orphan, process states, page replacement, threads vs processes, producer-consumer, deadlock fixing with lock ordering.
Ask which team before prepping networking depth: EOS/SONiC loops ask VRF, TCAM/ACLs, packet walk-throughs, netns/veth; generic backend loops only need DNS, TCP handshake, HTTP vs HTTPS/TLS.
Prepare a deep, whiteboard-able architecture story of your current project — the HM and director rounds are largely built on it.
Expect C or C++ to be forced in at least one round (campus rounds have been C-only); Java is accepted in some backend loops, Python is often unavailable even in the OA.
Negotiate hard with competing offers: reported first offers at 3 YOE ranged 29-37 LPA TC while negotiated outcomes hit 42-60 LPA at 3-4.5 YOE.
Don't read too much into a good round — fast binary verdicts, director resume reviews and position-filled rejections are all common; keep your pipeline warm.
process.notes: No bar-raiser or values round. OA platform is HackerRank (heavily proctored on campus; MCQs sometimes negatively marked). No classic FAANG-style HLD round for this band — 'system design' on the schedule usually turns out to be C++/OS depth, LLD, or a design-and-implement problem (one candidate prepped system design for a round that was entirely C++ virtual functions and bit manipulation). Interviews are CoderPad/Google Meet, with one in-person final common in India. Cool-off is ~1 year, and one 2024 report claims a prior-year rejection blocked rehire entirely. Compensation: base + anniversary bonus + USD RSUs vesting 25%/year over 4 years; ESPP exists; WLB and 2-day WFO cited as perks; several reports warn about low refresh/hikes in the India office.

dsa.title: Remove Linked List Elements
dsa.variant: Asked as void listRemove(Node **head, int v) — void return type forces careful double-pointer handling of head deletions; CoderPad came with a pre-written list harness and tests that had to pass.
dsa.evidence: Three independent experienced-hire reports (2023-04 senior SDE offer, 2024-02 Bengaluru offer, 2024-12 principal-engineer screen).

dsa.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
dsa.variant: Phrased as 'remove every node whose value repeats' (1→1→2→2→2→3→4→4 leaves only 3); complete a given function in VS Code and make it runnable.
dsa.evidence: Round 1 of a May 2026 C++ loop (cleared, then rejected on director resume review).

dsa.title: Missing Number (sorted-array variants)
dsa.variant: Recurring in several forms: sorted ascending array with one gap ({1..6,8,9}→7, {11,12,14,15,16}→13) where binary search is expected; sequence starting at an arbitrary number (and the interviewer made the candidate hand-implement lower_bound); unsorted n-1 consecutive integers (math answer accepted, then a hash-based one requested).
dsa.evidence: Four reports: 2026-05 round 1, 2025-04 Bengaluru DSA round, 2024-11 campus round 2, 2023-04 senior SDE round 1.

dsa.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
dsa.evidence: Two 2025 experienced-hire round-1 reports (4-YOE Oct 2025 screen; Aug 2025 DSA round alongside a doubly-linked-list design task).

dsa.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
dsa.variant: Warm-up before Insert Delete GetRandom in the same round; followed by HashMap-internals discussion.
dsa.evidence: Round 1 of a 2025 Golang backend loop (4.5 YOE, Bangalore).

dsa.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
dsa.variant: Also phrased as 'design a data structure supporting get, add, remove and getRandom in O(1)'.
dsa.evidence: Two 2025 reports: Golang backend round 1 (2025-07) and an Oct 2025 round 1 (alongside max-sum-of-k-consecutive).

dsa.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
dsa.variant: Paired both times with a find-the-deadlock code exercise; a TreeMap answer was accepted but over-complication was penalised.
dsa.evidence: Two senior-band Bengaluru reports: SDE-2 loop (2025-11) and Senior SWE round 1 (2026-02), both rejected.

dsa.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
dsa.variant: Asked first as 'count segments whose sum is zero', then generalised to any target sum. A sibling ask: longest subarray with a given sum including negatives (prefix-sum + first-index map), where missed edge cases sank the candidate.
dsa.evidence: SDE-2 round 1 (2025-07, Pune offer); longest-subarray form in a Jan 2025 SDE-2 round and a 2022 loop.

dsa.title: Sliding Window Maximum
dsa.variant: Paired with constructing a BST and coding node deletion in the same 1-hour round; running out of time on the second problem caused the rejection.
dsa.evidence: SDE-2 Bengaluru coding round, Feb 2024.

dsa.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
dsa.variant: Also asked as 'closest value to K in a BST' (return pointer to node with minimum absolute difference) in a 2024 intern round.
dsa.evidence: Off-campus SDE-1 round 1 (2026-01) and PICT Pune campus round 1 (2024-08).

dsa.title: BST with parent pointers: successor / predecessor / min / max / ordered traversal
dsa.variant: A signature Arista problem set: given struct node {value, left, right, parent}, complete findMin/findNext (inorder successor via parent links) and write inorder traversal using only those two; the mirror version asks findMax/findPrev/printReverse (descending print). Candidates who miss the parent pointer in the struct lose significant time. Also asked standalone as 'print a BST in descending order' and 'inorder traversal with and without recursion'.
dsa.evidence: Three reports: Feb 2024 Bengaluru offer (round 1), Dec 2024 Bangalore round 1, Jan 2024 round 1; descending-print also in the Feb 2024 HM round.

dsa.title: How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
dsa.evidence: Two reports two years apart: SDE-3 round 1 (2025-07) and a 6-YOE round 1 (2023-04).

dsa.title: Binary Tree Pruning (all-zero subtrees)
dsa.variant: Asked as 'remove all subtrees in which every node's value is 0' — post-order prune children, return null when value is 0 and both children are null.
dsa.evidence: SDE-3 round 1, 2025-07.

dsa.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
dsa.variant: Phrased as 'node X is special if no node on the root-to-X path has a greater value; count special nodes'.
dsa.evidence: 6-YOE round 1, 2023-04.

dsa.title: Valid Parentheses (coded in C)
dsa.variant: Expected in plain C (hand-rolled stack) right after pointer puzzles and memory-layout questions; campus version covered all bracket types.
dsa.evidence: Pune offer loop round 2 (2024-05) and PICT campus C-only round (2024-08).

dsa.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
dsa.variant: The plain version — max sum of k consecutive elements — was a 2025 round-1 warm-up; the distinct-elements version appeared in a 2024 DSA round and the 2025 intern OA.
dsa.evidence: Bengaluru offer round 1 (2024-05), Oct 2025 round 1 (plain variant), 2025-08 intern OA.

dsa.title: Find the Winner of the Circular Game (Josephus)
dsa.variant: O(n) time and O(1) space explicitly required — the simulation answer is not enough.
dsa.evidence: Bengaluru offer, DSA round, 2024-05.

dsa.title: Reverse Linked List II (reverse positions start..end)
dsa.variant: Given as start/end indices with several concrete cases including full-list reversal; working code from scratch, executed against every case.
dsa.evidence: 3.5-YOE Bengaluru technical round, 2024-07.

dsa.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
dsa.variant: Reported as 'pairwise rotate/swap alternate nodes of a linked list' in a 2026 round.
dsa.evidence: 2026-03 round-1 report (comment on prep thread) and 2024-08 intern round 1.

dsa.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane)
dsa.variant: First of three problems in a 2025 round 1 that opened with malloc/pointers and complexity warm-ups.
dsa.evidence: SWE round 1, 2025-07 (Red Hat SE2 candidate, cleared).

dsa.title: Min Stack (O(1) getMin)
dsa.variant: Design discussion only (auxiliary min-stack), no code required.
dsa.evidence: SWE round 1, 2025-07.

dsa.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
dsa.variant: Paired with Search in Rotated Sorted Array plus Java theory (singleton, static, final).
dsa.evidence: 4-YOE screen, 2025-10 (solved both, still rejected).

dsa.title: String to Integer (atoi)
dsa.variant: Asked in a screen that also probed debugging tools, sanitizers, SEGV and compilers.
dsa.evidence: 2025 technical screen report.

dsa.title: Word Ladder (+ Max Consecutive Ones III in same round)
dsa.variant: An outlier Java-backend round packing Word Ladder, Max Consecutive Ones III (LC 1004), Longest Word in Dictionary (LC 720), factory pattern and Java collections questions into one session — logic/approach level rather than full code for each.
dsa.evidence: 5.3-YOE backend round 1, 2024-04 (rejected).

dsa.title: LFU Cache (OA, exact)
dsa.variant: Verbatim LC 460 in the 2026 online assessment, alongside OS/bit-manipulation MCQs.
dsa.evidence: 2026 OA report.

dsa.title: Swap even and odd nibbles of a 32-bit integer
dsa.statement: Given a number such as 0x12345678, swap each even-positioned nibble with the adjacent odd nibble to produce 0x21436587. Solve with masks and shifts (mask the odd nibbles, mask the even nibbles, shift each by 4 and OR). Write full runnable code and explain each line.
dsa.evidence: Round 1 of a 2026 Bangalore SWE loop (4 YOE, EDA background).

dsa.title: Pair with given sum in a sorted doubly linked list
dsa.statement: Given a sorted doubly linked list (1↔2↔3↔4↔6↔8) and a target, output all pairs summing to the target (2+8, 4+6 for 10). Use head/tail two-pointer movement over the DLL. Follow-up: handle duplicate values without emitting duplicate pairs (skip equal neighbours while advancing).
dsa.evidence: Round 1 of a 2026 Bangalore SWE loop; full code run in an online IDE.

dsa.title: Split a circular linked list into two alternating lists in place
dsa.statement: Given a circular linked list 1→2→3→4→5→6(→1), produce two ordinary (non-circular) lists of the alternating nodes, 1→3→5 and 2→4→6, reusing the existing nodes — no new nodes or auxiliary lists. Full code from scratch; the interviewer also probed a segmentation fault the candidate hit (what SIGSEGV is, when and why it happens).
dsa.variant: Same round also asked binary tree vs BST and kth smallest in a BST.
dsa.evidence: Off-campus SDE-1 round 1, 2026-01.

dsa.title: Doubly linked list class: remove-all and positional insert
dsa.statement: Implement a doubly-linked-list class with two instance methods: removeAll(value) deleting every node holding the value, and insertAt(node, index) placing a node at a 0-indexed position — with the twist that if the node already exists in the list it must be moved (unlinked and relinked) to the target position. Complete working code expected.
dsa.variant: Followed by search-in-rotated-sorted-array, then Linux debugging commands and C++ template/STL grilling.
dsa.evidence: DSA round of an Aug 2025 loop.

dsa.title: Bit-manipulation drills: swap two bits; extract IPv4 octets
dsa.statement: Two recurring one-liners: (a) swap two given bit positions of an integer (test the bits; if they differ, flip both with an XOR mask), coded in an IDE and run against the interviewer's custom edge cases; (b) given a uint32 holding an IPv4 address, extract the four octets with shifts and 0xFF masks (bits 0-7, 8-15, 16-23, 24-31) and print the dotted address.
dsa.evidence: Swap-two-bits in a Jan 2024 round 1; octet extraction in a Jul 2024 Bengaluru round.

dsa.title: Add two unsigned chars into an unsigned int with manual carry
dsa.statement: Write a function taking two unsigned char values and returning their sum as an unsigned int, implementing the carry propagation yourself (bitwise half-adder loop: sum = a^b, carry = (a&b)<<1, repeat) instead of relying on integer promotion. The interviewer refused to give an example output — you must reason out the spec.
dsa.variant: Same round: predict output and object size of a class with virtual functions; compute the address of an array element as base + offset.
dsa.evidence: Second technical round ('system design' in name only), Nov 2024 Bangalore.

dsa.title: Find all occurrences of a target in a bitonic array in O(log n)
dsa.statement: Array first strictly increases then decreases ({1,3,81,79,21,15,11,5,3,1}); given a target (3), return the positions of all occurrences ({1,8}) in O(log n), without modifying the array or using extra space. Find the peak by binary search, then binary-search each half (the second half in descending order).
dsa.evidence: SSE India round 1 (2023-01), echoed in a 2020 campus round (find element in bitonic array, linear then optimised).

dsa.title: Phone-number autocomplete with a Trie
dsa.statement: Build autocomplete over phone numbers (or a telephone directory of name+number): implement insertion and prefix search over a digit trie, plus a main() that exercises it, and run it live. The directory variant requires returning all names starting with a typed prefix. Candidates are expected to identify the trie themselves from a vague prompt.
dsa.variant: Arista leans on tries repeatedly — see also the firewall IP-range matcher in LLD.
dsa.evidence: Round 1 2025-07 (CoderPad, C++); directory variant in an Apr 2024 round.

dsa.title: Zigzag-rearrange a linked list (a<b>c<d>e)
dsa.statement: Rearrange a singly linked list so values alternate a < b > c < d > e in a single O(n) pass: walk the list and, whenever the required inequality at the current pair is violated, swap the two node values (or relink), flipping the comparison each step.
dsa.evidence: Intern technical round 1, 2025-08 (same loop asked C pointers and ls | grep).

dsa.title: OA 2026: maximum total server processing time
dsa.statement: numTasks tasks with processTime[i] are split so each of numServer servers gets a contiguous block of at least m tasks; a server's processing time is the sum of its m largest task times; servers run sequentially. Maximise the total. Looks like partition DP but the accepted answer is greedy: sort descending and sum the global top numServer*m values.
dsa.evidence: 2026 online assessment (Bangalore SWE loop).

dsa.title: OA 2026: minimum merges to make an array a palindrome
dsa.statement: One operation replaces two adjacent elements with their sum; find the minimum operations to make the array a palindrome ([12,14,8,13,5]→3). Two pointers from both ends: when ends are equal move inward, otherwise merge the smaller end into its neighbour and count an operation.
dsa.evidence: 2026 online assessment (Bangalore SWE loop).

dsa.title: OA 2026: API bandwidth allocation (0/1 knapsack)
dsa.statement: Given total available bandwidth, each API endpoint's bandwidth requirement and the number of requests it can resolve, choose endpoints to maximise requests resolved within the bandwidth budget — a direct 0/1 knapsack (capacity=bandwidth, weight=endpoint bandwidth, value=requests).
dsa.variant: Same OA had LFU Cache verbatim and MCQs on fork counts, FIFO page faults, hashing collisions, XOR and loop complexity.
dsa.evidence: 2026 online assessment report.

dsa.title: C pointer reseat puzzle: p=&x vs *p=x
dsa.statement: Given void function(int *p){ int x=100; p=&x; } called with a pointer to a=10, predict the printed *ptr (10 — the parameter copy is reseated, the caller's pointer is untouched) and then fix the function so it prints 100 (*p = x). The follow-up in 2026 added an output question on object destruction order and how stack memory is laid out for the class.
dsa.evidence: Verbatim in an Oct 2025 round and reused in a May 2026 round 1 (the later post links the earlier one as 'the same question').

dsa.title: Debug a short C program (stack-return, sizeof, uninitialised)
dsa.statement: Live-debug a small C file with three planted bugs: an uninitialised accumulator in sum(), an input() function returning a pointer to a local (stack) array, and sizeof(a) applied to a pointer parameter instead of passing the length. Identify all three, explain stack vs heap, then rewrite with malloc. Composure matters: the interviewer reacted badly to a printf left inside a loop.
dsa.variant: A US intern version: find 3-4 bugs in a short C++ program and reuse functions built earlier in the interview.
dsa.evidence: SONiC round 2 (2025-07); C++ intern variant (2025 comment).

dsa.title: Implement strlen() / memcpy() in C
dsa.statement: Write the libc functions from scratch: strlen (walk to the NUL terminator) and memcpy (byte-wise copy via unsigned char*; be ready to discuss alignment, word-wise copying and what memmove adds for overlapping ranges). Asked cold, in C, inside otherwise conversational rounds.
dsa.evidence: strlen in a 2025 screen; memcpy in the 2024-05 Pune hiring-manager round.

dsa.title: Implement your own free() — how does free know the size?
dsa.statement: After discussing how malloc/new work, explain how free knows how many bytes to release (allocator metadata header stored before the returned pointer) and sketch your own free implementation that reads the header and returns the block to a free list. Part of an OS-focused round that began by debugging a stack-overflow recursion over SSH.
dsa.evidence: Hiring-manager round, Feb 2024 Bengaluru offer.

dsa.title: Find and fix the deadlock in a transfer snippet
dsa.statement: Given a small code snippet where thread A transfers money to B while B simultaneously transfers to A (each locking its own account then the other's), identify the deadlock, explain the four conditions, and fix it. A single global lock is marked down — the expected fix is fine-grained locking with a consistent lock ordering (e.g., lock accounts by id order) or try-lock with back-off.
dsa.evidence: SDE-2 round 1 (2025-11, rejected for proposing a global lock) and Senior SWE round 1 (2026-02).

dsa.title: Process memory layout, stack overflow and virtual memory
dsa.statement: Recurring cluster: given an infinitely recursing function (func(b--) never terminating), explain what happens at runtime — walk the text/data/bss/heap/stack layout, what stack overflow is and how the kernel detects it, then into virtual memory and paging. Variants: 'does while(1){} overflow the stack?' (no — no frame growth), where static/const/global variables live, static vs dynamic vs register allocation, struct padding and linked-list cache locality.
dsa.evidence: SSH-into-vim exercise in the Feb 2024 HM round; while(1) in Jul 2024; storage-class questions in 2024-01, PICT 2024 and a Jun 2026 Glassdoor report (struct padding, cache locality).

dsa.title: Virtual functions: vtable, object size, output prediction
dsa.statement: Given a class hierarchy with virtual functions, predict the program output and sizeof the object, explaining the vptr/vtable; follow-ups cover virtual destructors, destruction order and how the compiler lays the object out. Asked both as standalone quizzes and inside rounds labelled 'system design'.
dsa.variant: Interns get 'how do virtual functions work at the compiler level' and object slicing.
dsa.evidence: Nov 2024 Bangalore round; May 2026 round 1 (destructor/memory-layout variant); 2025-08 intern round.

dsa.title: unordered_map / HashMap internals
dsa.statement: Explain how std::unordered_map / Java HashMap works inside: bucket array, hash-to-bucket mapping, collision handling (chaining vs open addressing), load factor, how bucket count is chosen and how the table grows/rehashes. Reliably asked as a follow-up right after you use a hash map in a coding answer.
dsa.evidence: Director round Feb 2024, round 1 Jul 2025, SDE-1 round 2 Jan 2026, PICT round 1 2024, intern round 2 2025 (then 'implement a hash map class').

dsa.title: Processes, threads and scheduling Q&A
dsa.statement: Standing OS battery: process vs thread (memory sharing, context-switch cost, IPC options), fork vs exec and what happens when exec fails, zombie vs orphan processes with a timeline scenario (main forks at 5s and sleeps to 100s, child finishes at 25s — give both states), process states, concurrency vs parallelism on multicore. A quantitative favourite: will 8 threads beat 4 threads processing a 100GB file on a 4-core machine, and why not. Producer-consumer synchronisation chains also appear.
dsa.evidence: Campus round 1 2024-11 (fork/exec/zombie grilling), Pune loop 2024-05 (thread vs process IPC, producer-consumer), 2026-08 round 1 (concurrency vs parallelism, multicore), SSE round 2023-01 (8-vs-4 threads).

dsa.title: Networking fundamentals Q&A (DNS, TCP, TLS, sockets)
dsa.statement: Core battery for every team: how DNS resolution works; what happens when you type a URL (DNS → TCP three-way handshake → request/response); HTTP vs HTTPS and how TLS/SSL encrypts (who encrypts at the browser end, certificates, key exchange); how a server on one port distinguishes clients — socket multiplexing/demultiplexing by 4-tuple; OSI layers in detail; 'how would you debug a slow API'. Depth of follow-ups is the differentiator, not the topics.
dsa.evidence: Pune loop 2024-05 (DNS), SDE-1 round 2 2026-01 (sockets/multiplexing/OSI), SDE-2 2025-11 (how HTTPS works), Senior SWE 2026-02 (TLS + slow-API debugging), SSE 2023-01 (SSL/HTTP).

dsa.title: Switch internals and Linux network namespaces (EOS/SONiC teams)
dsa.statement: For networking-team loops, a 40-45 minute block: what VRF is and how it works; how CAM/TCAM store and match ACLs in hardware; what happens when a packet's MAC is rewritten; the full per-hop life of a packet including next-hop resolution and ACL effects. Then a practical: simulate Host1→Router1→Router2→Host2 on one Linux machine using network namespaces and veth pairs, assigning IPs and routes.
dsa.variant: Team context also included eBPF, ECMP and ASIC-level debugging discussion.
dsa.evidence: SONiC round 2, 2025-07 (cleared).

dsa.title: Linux practical and debugging-tooling questions
dsa.statement: Scattered through rounds: how to find files with duplicate content in a directory (hash each file, dedupe via a map — then the unordered_map internals follow-up); kill -9 <pid> and signal semantics; what ls | grep does; Linux debugging commands; gdb, sanitizers, what SIGSEGV means and common causes; what happens internally when ls runs (fork/exec/syscalls) and kernel vs user space.
dsa.evidence: Director round Feb 2024, Apr 2024 round, 2025 screen (sanitizers/SEGV), Aug 2025 DSA round (Linux debugging commands), PICT round 3 2024 (ls internals).

dsa.title: C++/Java language-depth grilling
dsa.statement: Language round-outs by stack: C++ — templates and STL details, RAII, smart pointers, virtual functions, the diamond problem, shallow vs deep copy, printf('x') vs printf("x") memory semantics; Java — singleton, static/final keywords, Vector vs ArrayList, pass-by-value quiz (funA(int a){a++}, funB(int[] a){a[0]=1}, funC(Object c){c.value++} — what does main observe), garbage collector internals. Weakness here is a stated rejection reason even when coding went well.
dsa.evidence: Pune director round 2024-05 (RAII/smart pointers), Aug 2025 round (templates/STL), SDE-2 2025-07 (Java pass-by-value quiz), 2025-10 screen (singleton/static/final), 2023-11 round 2 (diamond problem).

design.title: Deep dive: architecture of your own current project
design.prompt: Walk through the architecture of a system you built or own today — components, data flow, why each technology was chosen.
probes: why this DB / message queue and not alternatives
how it scales and where it breaks
failure handling and operational war stories
HTTP basics, data modelling, transactions, cloud usage
interviewers (HM and director) are deep and will drill until you run out of depth
design.evidence: The one constant across nearly every experienced loop: 2023-04 HM+director rounds, 2024-05 director round, 2025-07 (both SDE-2 and Golang loops), 2025-11 SDE-2.

design.title: Design an e-commerce system (whiteboard)
design.prompt: Open-ended: design an e-commerce platform end to end on a whiteboard, after discussing your past projects.
probes: in-depth discussion across multiple areas (catalog, cart, orders, payments)
both HLD and LLD level expected in one session
design.evidence: SDE-2 Pune loop 2025-07 (offer extended straight after this round); a second candidate reports 'HLD and LLD of ecommerce' as their round 2 (2025-08 comment).

design.title: Top-K log analysis across servers
design.prompt: Multiple servers receive logs recording which (IP, port) called the system and what packets were sent. Support queries like 'highest-volume IP' and 'which server handles the most load'.
probes: time and space complexity of every operation
scaling from one box to the fleet
design.evidence: Aug 2025 HM round (30 min resume/Linux + 60 min on this).

design.title: Design a Coursera-like course platform with enterprise licensing
design.prompt: Design an online-courses system where enterprises license course bundles for employees; focus on the licensing/entitlement path.
probes: race conditions on license grab and locking strategy
database choice and schema in detail
design.evidence: Bengaluru offer loop, 2024-05 (round after the firewall LLD).

design.title: Design an online Snakes & Ladders game server
design.prompt: Design a gaming server that hosts multiplayer Snakes & Ladders games.
probes: paired with Java/C++ language questions (diamond problem) in the same round
a 2022 loop followed it with generic HLD questions
design.evidence: Two reports: SDE-2 Bengaluru 2023-11 and a 2022 loop (offer).

design.title: Design an MMU (memory management unit)
design.prompt: Design how a memory management unit translates and manages memory — page tables, TLB, fault handling.
probes: fits Arista's OS-heavy bar rather than web-scale HLD
design.round: Campus technical round (asked to the poster's batchmates)
design.evidence: Second-hand within a detailed 2024-11 campus report.

lld.title: Parking lot with concurrency
lld.prompt: Low-level design of a parking lot system: core entities, classes, allocation logic — and explicitly how you handle concurrent entry/exit.
lld.deliverable: class design + key methods discussed live; concurrency handling reasoned through
lld.evidence: 2025-07 Golang loop round 2 (positive feedback); a 2025-11 commenter confirms 'generic LLD questions like Parking Lot' for the EOS round 2.

lld.title: License management system (interval queries)
lld.prompt: Design a license manager that can fetch all licenses valid between two dates (x, y) and find licenses about to expire to send notifications.
lld.deliverable: data-structure-centric design; hash map first, then efficient range structure
probes: efficient date-range querying — interviewer steered toward an interval tree
a 2025-11 commenter says start/end-time range-query structures are 'their favourite question'
lld.round: Face-to-face round 2 with engineering manager (90 min)
lld.evidence: Oct 2025 round 2 (rejected on this); corroborated by EOS round-2 guidance comment (2025-11).

lld.title: Firewall: allow/deny by IP ranges (trie)
lld.prompt: Design and implement a firewall that decides allow/deny for a request given configured source and destination IP ranges.
lld.deliverable: working trie implementation coded in the round
probes: why a hashmap of ranges is too costly
bit-trie over IPs; merging source+destination into one trie

lld.title: URL shortener as pure LLD (no database)
lld.prompt: Design a URL shortener supporting custom and auto-generated aliases — but as classes/interfaces/attributes/methods only: no databases, just in-memory data structures behind APIs.
lld.deliverable: class design: which APIs exist, what data models they touch, how structures mutate per call
probes: how each API call manipulates your structures

lld.title: Router ID allocator library
lld.prompt: A router assigns IDs (>= 0) to devices that connect and must free them on disconnect. Design a library with assign/free functions optimising both time and space.
lld.deliverable: class structure + data-structure choice defended under requirement questioning
probes: accepted answer: counter for fresh IDs + free list (linked list) for recycled ones

lld.title: Singleton + immutable class
lld.prompt: Implement a thread-safe singleton; then, given Address and Person (name + List<Address>) classes, make Person immutable.
lld.deliverable: working code; correctness of the immutability contract
probes: final fields, no setters — and the getter must return an immutable/defensive copy of the list (the usual trap)
theory follow-ups: static, final, enum singletons
lld.evidence: SDE-2 round 1 2025-01 (rejected over edge cases here); singleton theory again in 2025-10 screen and an Apr 2024 round.

lld.title: Implement a dynamic array (vector) in C
lld.prompt: Build std::vector in plain C: allocation with malloc/realloc, growth policy, element access; interviewer supplies inputs to test behaviour.
lld.deliverable: working code run against interviewer-provided input

lld.title: Implement a hash map class
lld.prompt: Design and implement a hash map from scratch: bucket array, hash function, and collision resolution.
lld.deliverable: class implementation (campus: full; experienced: approach + key methods)
probes: follow-up ties into the standing unordered_map-internals question
lld.round: Technical round 2 (intern/campus); internals Q&A version for experienced
lld.evidence: Intern round 2 2025-08 ('implement a hash-map class' after ordered_map internals); hash-map-via-arrays approach in the 2020 campus final; internals asked of experienced hires repeatedly.

lld.title: Design and implement malloc() in C
lld.prompt: Write your own malloc: choose the bookkeeping structure, implement allocation and free, and handle fragmentation.
lld.deliverable: working design + code with interviewer hints
lld.evidence: PICT Pune campus round 4, 2024-08 (offer); pairs with the recurring implement-free() ask in experienced loops.

lld.title: Parallelise a hot image-download function
lld.prompt: A function that downloads images is called thousands of times; optimise it.
